Bacterial Leaf Blight.name: Bacterial Leaf Blight
Bacterial Leaf Blight.description: Bacterial Leaf Blight (BLB) is one of the most destructive bacterial diseases affecting rice worldwide. It infects rice plants at all growth stages and is especially severe during warm, humid, and rainy conditions. The disease enters the plant through wounds or natural openings such as hydathodes and rapidly spreads through the vascular tissues, blocking water movement. As the infection progresses, leaves turn yellow, dry out, and eventually die. Severe infections can reduce grain yield by 20% to 80%, depending on the rice variety, environmental conditions, and stage of infection. Early diagnosis and proper field management are essential to minimize economic losses.
Bacterial Leaf Blight.history: Bacterial Leaf Blight was first reported in Japan in the late nineteenth century and has since become one of the most economically important rice diseases throughout Asia, including India, Bangladesh, China, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Bacterial Leaf Blight.economic_importance: The disease can cause significant reductions in grain yield, poor grain quality, and increased production costs due to repeated chemical applications.
Bacterial Leaf Blight.cause: Caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae.
Bacterial Leaf Blight.disease_cycle: The bacteria survive in infected crop residues, volunteer rice plants, weeds, irrigation water, and infected seeds. Rain splashes, wind, irrigation water, and contaminated farm equipment spread the bacteria to healthy plants.
symptoms: Yellow water-soaked streaks along leaf edges
Leaves gradually dry from the tip downward
Milky bacterial ooze may appear in humid conditions
early_stage: Small yellow streaks near leaf tips
medicine_usage: Mix Copper Oxychloride according to manufacturer instructions.
Repeat every 7 to 10 days if symptoms continue.
expert_tips: Early detection significantly reduces yield loss.
Inspect fields every week during rainy seasons.
Do not move infected plant material to healthy fields.

Brown Spot.name: Brown Spot
Brown Spot.description: Brown Spot is one of the oldest known fungal diseases of rice. It attacks leaves, leaf sheaths, glumes, and grains. The disease commonly develops in nutrient-deficient soils and during periods of drought stress. Brown Spot reduces photosynthesis, weakens the plant, and lowers grain quality. Severe infections may reduce yields by 40% or more if not managed properly.
Brown Spot.history: Brown Spot gained worldwide attention after contributing to the Bengal Famine of 1943 by severely reducing rice production.
Brown Spot.economic_importance: The disease reduces both grain quantity and grain quality, leading to major economic losses in rice-producing regions.
Brown Spot.cause: Caused by the fungus Bipolaris oryzae.
Brown Spot.disease_cycle: The fungus survives on infected seeds, crop residues, and soil. Spores spread through wind and rain splash.
medicine_usage: Spray at first appearance of symptoms.
expert_tips: Brown Spot is commonly associated with nutrient deficiency.
Healthy soil significantly reduces disease severity.

Healthy Rice Leaf.name: Healthy Rice Leaf
Healthy Rice Leaf.description: The rice plant is healthy and free from visible symptoms of diseases or pest infestations. Healthy rice leaves are bright green, upright, smooth, and capable of efficient photosynthesis. Maintaining healthy plants through balanced fertilization, proper irrigation, and routine monitoring is essential for achieving maximum grain yield and quality. Although no disease is detected, continuous observation is recommended because environmental stress and pathogens can quickly affect plant health.
Healthy Rice Leaf.history: Healthy rice plants indicate successful crop management practices and favorable environmental conditions.
Healthy Rice Leaf.economic_importance: Healthy plants produce maximum grain yield, better grain quality, and higher farmer income.
expert_tips: Healthy plants should still be inspected weekly.
Preventive management is always better than curative treatment.

Leaf Blast.name: Leaf Blast
Leaf Blast.description: Leaf Blast is one of the most devastating fungal diseases of rice worldwide. It attacks leaves, nodes, collars, and panicles. Under favorable conditions, especially high humidity and frequent rainfall, the fungus spreads rapidly through airborne spores. Initial infections begin as small gray-green lesions that later develop into characteristic diamond-shaped spots with gray centers and brown margins. Severe infections reduce photosynthesis, weaken plants, and significantly reduce grain production. Without proper management, Leaf Blast can destroy large areas of rice fields within a short period.
Leaf Blast.history: Leaf Blast has been recognized for over 300 years and remains one of the most economically important rice diseases worldwide.
Leaf Blast.economic_importance: Yield losses range from 10% to over 80% depending on the severity of infection and environmental conditions.
Leaf Blast.cause: Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae.
Leaf Blast.disease_cycle: The fungus survives on infected crop residues, volunteer rice plants, weeds, and seeds. Airborne spores spread rapidly during humid weather and infect healthy leaves through moisture on the leaf surface.
medicine_usage: Apply fungicide immediately after the first symptoms appear.
Repeat every 10 to 14 days if necessary.
expert_tips: Leaf Blast spreads rapidly during humid weather.
Early fungicide application is the most effective control strategy.
Weekly field inspection can prevent severe outbreaks.

Leaf Scald.name: Leaf Scald
Leaf Scald.description: Leaf Scald is a fungal disease that affects rice leaves, reducing photosynthesis and weakening plant growth. The disease begins as small water-soaked lesions near the leaf tip or edge. These lesions enlarge into irregular grayish-white or straw-colored patches surrounded by dark brown margins, giving the leaf a scorched appearance. Under warm and humid conditions, the fungus spreads rapidly through rain splash and wind. Although Leaf Scald is generally less destructive than Rice Blast, severe infections can reduce grain filling, lower grain quality, and decrease overall yield.
Leaf Scald.history: Leaf Scald has been reported in rice-growing countries throughout Asia, Africa, and South America. It is more common in fields with poor drainage and high humidity.
Leaf Scald.economic_importance: Yield losses usually range from 5% to 25%, but severe outbreaks can cause higher losses when environmental conditions remain favorable.
Leaf Scald.cause: Caused by the fungus Microdochium oryzae.
Leaf Scald.disease_cycle: The fungus survives in infected crop residues and infected seeds. Spores spread through rain splash, irrigation water, and wind.
medicine_usage: Spray fungicide immediately after symptoms appear.
expert_tips: Regular scouting is recommended during rainy weather.

Narrow Brown Leaf Spot.name: Narrow Brown Leaf Spot
Narrow Brown Leaf Spot.description: Narrow Brown Leaf Spot is a fungal disease characterized by long, narrow, dark brown streaks on rice leaves. The disease mainly affects older leaves but may spread throughout the canopy under humid conditions. Severe infections reduce photosynthesis, weaken plant growth, and lower grain yield. Although often confused with Brown Spot, the lesions are much narrower and elongated.
Narrow Brown Leaf Spot.history: The disease is commonly reported in tropical and subtropical rice-growing regions where humidity remains high for extended periods.
Narrow Brown Leaf Spot.economic_importance: Yield losses generally range from 5% to 30% depending on disease severity and environmental conditions.
Narrow Brown Leaf Spot.cause: Caused by the fungus Cercospora janseana.
Narrow Brown Leaf Spot.disease_cycle: The fungus survives on infected crop debris and seeds. Spores are spread by wind, rain splash, and irrigation water.
medicine_usage: Spray every 10–14 days until disease is controlled.
expert_tips: Scout fields every week during humid weather.

Rice Hispa.name: Rice Hispa
Rice Hispa.description: Rice Hispa is one of the most destructive insect pests of rice. Both adults and larvae feed on rice leaves, reducing the green leaf area available for photosynthesis. Adult beetles scrape the upper surface of leaves, creating long white streaks, while larvae mine inside the leaf tissue. Severe infestations weaken plants, delay growth, reduce tillering, and ultimately decrease grain yield. Outbreaks are more common during warm and humid weather and in poorly managed rice fields.
Rice Hispa.history: Rice Hispa has been reported throughout South and Southeast Asia and remains an important insect pest in rice-growing regions.
Rice Hispa.economic_importance: Heavy infestations can reduce grain yield by 20–50% depending on crop stage and severity.
Rice Hispa.life_cycle: Adult females lay eggs inside leaf tissue. Larvae feed by mining inside leaves before pupating. Adults emerge and continue feeding on leaf surfaces.
medicine_usage: Repeat after 10–14 days if infestation persists.
expert_tips: Early insecticide application prevents severe outbreaks.

Sheath Blight.name: Sheath Blight
Sheath Blight.description: Sheath Blight is one of the most important fungal diseases of rice. It attacks the leaf sheath, leaves, and stems near the water level. The disease begins as small green-gray lesions that enlarge into oval lesions with brown borders. Under humid conditions, the fungus spreads rapidly from plant to plant through direct contact. Severe infections weaken stems, reduce grain filling, increase lodging, and significantly decrease yield. Dense planting and excessive nitrogen fertilizer greatly increase disease severity.
Sheath Blight.history: Sheath Blight has become increasingly important with the adoption of high-yielding rice varieties and intensive fertilizer use.
Sheath Blight.economic_importance: Yield losses typically range from 10% to 50%, but severe epidemics may cause even greater losses.
Sheath Blight.cause: Caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani.
Sheath Blight.disease_cycle: The fungus survives in soil and infected crop residues as sclerotia. Under warm, humid conditions it infects lower leaf sheaths and spreads upward through plant contact.
early_stage: Small green-gray lesions near water level
expert_tips: Maintain good airflow within the crop canopy.
Early fungicide application provides the best control.
